arXiv:1312.0252v2 [math.AP] 07 Feb 2015

Boundary spikes of a Keller–Segel chemotaxis system with saturated logarithmic sensitivity

Qi Wang ††thanks: (Email:qwang@swufe.edu.cn). Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics Affiliation: 555 Liutai Ave, Wenjiang, Chengdu, Sichuan 611130, China
Abstract

In this paper, we study the nonconstant positive steady states of a Keller-Segel chemotaxis system over a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset{R}^{N}, N≥1N\geq 1. The sensitivity function is chosen to be ϕ⁡(v)=ln⁡(v+c)\phi(v)=\ln(v+c) where cc is a positive constant. For the chemical diffusion rate being small, we construct positive solutions with a boundary spike supported on a platform. Moreover, this spike approaches the most curved part of the boundary of the domain as the chemical diffusion rate shrinks to zero. We also conduct extensive numerical simulations to illustrate the formation of stable boundary and interior spikes of the system. These spiky solutions can be used to model the self–organized cell aggregation phenomenon in chemotaxis.

Competition model, shadow system, nonlinear boundary value problem, transition layer.

1

1 Introduction and main result

Chemotaxis is the oriented movement of cells along the gradient of certain chemicals in their environment. One of the most interesting phenomena in chemotaxis is the cell aggregation and it is an important mechanism for the formation of a fruiting body from single cells. See [7, 14] and [15] for detailed discussions. This phenomenon has been discovered in bacteria, in particular E. coli, and also in the cell slime molds such as Dictyostelium discoideum. See [2, 7] and the references therein. One of the main reasons of the directed movements of the cells is that they can navigate within a complex environment by detecting and processing of a variety of internal and external signals. Certain chemicals, most frequently inorganic salt, amino acids and some proteins called chemokines, can induce chemotaxis in motile cells.

In this paper we study the existence of nonconstant positive solutions (u,v)=(u⁡(x),v⁡(x))(u,v)=(u(x),v(x)) to the following system

{∇⋅(∇u−pu∇ln(v+c))=0,x∈Ω,ϵ2​Δ​v−v+β​u/α=0,x∈Ω,∂u∂n=∂v∂n=0,x∈∂Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\nabla\cdot(\nabla u-pu\nabla\ln(v+c))=0,&x\in\Omega,\\ \epsilon^{2}\Delta v-v+\beta u/\alpha=0,&x\in\Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\textbf{n}}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\textbf{n}}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\end{array}\right. (1.1)

where Ω\Omega is a bounded domain in ℝN{R}^{N}, N≥1N\geq 1, with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega. n is the unit outer normal on the boundary. The parameters pp, cc, ϵ\epsilon, α\alpha and β\beta are assumed to be positive constants. Let uu be the cellular population density and vv be the chemical concentration, then system (1.1) can be used to model the steady state of a chemotaxis system with saturated logarithmic sensitivity function. We are concerned with boundary spike solutions to (1.1) and our main theorem goes as follows.

Furthermore, PϵP_{\epsilon} approaches the most curved part of the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega in the sense that H⁡(Pϵ)→maxP∈∂Ω⁡H⁡(P)H(P_{\epsilon})\rightarrow\max_{P\in\partial\Omega}H(P), where H⁡(P)H(P) is the mean curvature of the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega at point PP.

The mathematical modeling of chemotaxis was initiated by Keller and Segel in their pioneering works [16, 17, 18] during 1970s. Denote by u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) the cell population density and by v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) the chemical concentration at space–time (x,t)(x,t). Then the general Keller–Segel model reads as follows

{ut=∇⋅(d1(u,v)∇u−χ(u,v)∇ϕ(v)),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=d2​(u,v)​Δ​v+k⁡(u,v),x∈Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x)≥0,v(x,0)=v0(x)≥0,x∈Ω,∂u∂n=∂v∂n=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(d_{1}(u,v)\nabla u-\chi(u,v)\nabla\phi(v)),&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ v_{t}=d_{2}(u,v)\Delta v+k(u,v),&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0,v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0,&x\in\Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\textbf{n}}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\textbf{n}}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,~t>0,\\ \end{array}\right. (1.3)

where d1,d2>0d_{1},d_{2}>0 are the diffusion rates of cells and chemicals respectively and χ⁡(u,v)\chi(u,v) is a function that measures the chemotactic response of cells to the chemical. Moreover, χ\chi is positive if the chemical is chemo–attractive (sugar, nutrition, etc.) to the cells and it is negative if the chemical is chemo–repulsive (poison, toxin for example). ϕ⁡(v)>0\phi(v)>0 is the so–called (signal–dependent) sensitivity function and it reflects the variance of cellular sensitivity with respect to the chemical concentration. k⁡(u,v)k(u,v) is the creation and degradation rate of the chemical. The non–flux boundary conditions mean that the domain Ω\Omega is enclosed thus it inhibits cell immigration and chemical diffusion across the boundary. The nonnegative initial data u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} are not identically zero.

Keller–Segel system (1.3) and its variants have been studied extensively over the past few decades. These systems are very rich in mathematical dynamics and they can induce many interesting and striking properties such as global solutions, finite time blow–ups, traveling waves, etc. Furthermore, the intuitively simple system (1.3), even in its simplest form, successfully demonstrates its ability in presenting solutions with self–organized spatial patterns with concentration properties such as boundary spike or interior spike. These spiky solutions can be used to model the aforementioned cellular aggregation and concentration phenomena. See the survey paper [12] for detailed discussions.

From the viewpoint of mathematical modeling, we say that cells aggregate if there exists a solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) that converges to a nonconstant positive function u⁡(x)u(x),

limt→Tu⁡(x,t)=u⁡(x),T≤∞.\lim_{t\rightarrow T}u(x,t)=u(x),T\leq\infty.

In this paper, we focus on the interplay between the sensitivity function ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) and the terms d1d_{1}, d2d_{2} and χ\chi on the mathematical modeling of cell aggregations phenomenon. To make our goal evident, we assume that d1d_{1} and d2d_{2} are positive constants and k⁡(u,v)=−α​v+β​uk(u,v)=-\alpha v+\beta u for some positive constants α\alpha and β\beta. Under these settings, Keller–Segel model (1.3) becomes

{ut=∇⋅(d1∇u−χu∇ϕ(v)),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=d2​Δ​v−α​v+β​u,x∈Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x)≥0,v(x,0)=v0(x)≥0,x∈Ω,∂u∂n=∂v∂n=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(d_{1}\nabla u-\chi u\nabla\phi(v)),&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ v_{t}=d_{2}\Delta v-\alpha v+\beta u,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0,~v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0,&x\in\Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\textbf{n}}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\textbf{n}}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,~t>0,\end{array}\right. (1.4)

and we want to find nonconstant positive steady states to systems in the form of (1.4).

Time–dependent system (1.4) can model cell aggregation if L∞L_{\infty}–norm of the solutions goes to infinity, then the aggregation is simulated by a δ\delta–function or a linear combination of δ\delta-functions that represents the chemical concentration. The formal study of blow–up solutions of Keller-Segel models was initiated in [5, 25] and the local profile of the blow–ups was rigourously constructed in [11] over a 2D domain. Though such blow–up solutions are evidently connected to the phenomenon of cellular aggregation, a δ\delta–function is not the optimal choice from the viewpoint of mathematical modeling. It challenges the rationality that chemical concentration can not be infinity at a spot in the domain and it also brings difficulties to numerical simulations. Moreover, rigourous analysis of the states after blow–up is impossible. An alternative approach available in the literature is to show that positive solutions of (1.4) exist globally in time and converge to bounded steady states as time increases. Then the steady states with concentrating properties such as spikes, transition layers, etc. can be used to describe the cell aggregation phenomenon. We shall take the second approach in our paper and it is the goal of the current work to investigate the existence of nonconstant positive steady states of system (1.4).

For N=1N=1, it has been well known that solutions to (1.4) and a collection of its variants are global and bounded in time. See [13, 30] for example. However, the global existence is not always available for higher dimensional domains. It turns out that the sensitivity function ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) and system parameters in (1.4) play essential roles in existence of its global–in–time solutions. Two most commonly used sensitivity functions are ϕ⁡(v)=v\phi(v)=v and ϕ=ln⁡v\phi=\ln v, which lead (1.4) to the so–called minimal model and logarithmic model respectively. See the survey paper of Hillen and Painter [12].

For ϕ⁡(v)=v\phi(v)=v, Nagai, et al. [23] established the global solutions (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))(u(x,t),v(x,t)) of (1.4) with d1=d2=1d_{1}=d_{2}=1 over Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset{R}^{2}, if either ∫Ωu0​(x)​𝑑x<4​π/(β​χ)\int_{\Omega}u_{0}(x)dx<4\pi/(\beta\chi), or ∫Ωu0​(x)​𝑑x<8​π/(β​χ)\int_{\Omega}u_{0}(x)dx<8\pi/(\beta\chi), Ω\Omega is a disk and (u0​(x),v0​(x))(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x)) is radial in xx. Winkler [39] studied the same problem with d1=d2=χ=α=β=1d_{1}=d_{2}=\chi=\alpha=\beta=1 over Ω⊂ℝN,N≥3\Omega\subset{R}^{N},N\geq 3. It has been proved that the solutions of (1.4) exist globally in time provided that ‖u0​(x)‖LN/2+δ\|u_{0}(x)\|_{L^{N/2+\delta}} and ‖∇v0​(x)‖LN+δ\|\nabla v_{0}(x)\|_{L^{N+\delta}} are small for some δ>0\delta>0.

For ϕ⁡(v)=ln⁡v\phi(v)=\ln v, Nagai, et al. [24] established the global solutions of (1.4) with d1=d2=α=β=1d_{1}=d_{2}=\alpha=\beta=1 over Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset{R}^{2} provided that either χ<1\chi<1 or χ<5/2\chi<5/2, Ω\Omega is a disk and (u0​(x),v0​(x))(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x)) is radial in xx. Winkler [40] studied the same problem and established the global classical solutions over Ω⊂ℝN,N≥2\Omega\subset{R}^{N},N\geq 2 if χ<2/N\chi<\sqrt{2/N} and global weak solutions if χ<(N+2)/(3​N−4)\chi<\sqrt{(N+2)/(3N-4)}. Furthermore, Nagai and Senba [22] proved the global existence and boundedness for the parabolic–elliptic system of (1.4) when Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset{R}^{2} is a disk and (u0​(x),v0​(x))(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x)) is radial, or χ<2\chi<2, Ω⊂ℝ3\Omega\subset{R}^{3} is a ball and (u0​(x),v0​(x))(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x)) is radial. An exploration of literatures suggests that both the smallness of initial data and of the chemo–attraction rate χ\chi tend to prevent solutions of (1.4) from blowing up in finite or infinite time.

Attempts have been made to show that the steady states of (1.4) have concentrating properties such as boundary spikes, interior spikes, etc., when the chemical diffusion rate is sufficiently small. This approach was initiated by Lin, Ni and Takagi in a series of remarkable papers [20, 28, 29] around 1990s. To be precise, their pioneering works focus on the logarithmic case ϕ⁡(v)=ln⁡v\phi(v)=\ln v and can be summarized as follows. Through the transformation introduced in [31] and proper parameter scalings, the stationary system of (1.4) reduces to the following single equation

d2Δv−v+vp=0,x∈Ω,∇v⋅n=0,x∈∂Ω,d_{2}\Delta v-v+v^{p}=0,x\in\Omega,~~\nabla v\cdot\textbf{n}=0,~x\in\partial\Omega, (1.5)

where p=χd1p=\frac{\chi}{d_{1}}. Equation (1.5) is associated with an energy functional

Jd2:=12​∫Ω(d2​|∇v|2+v2)​𝑑x−1p+1​∫Ωv+p+1​𝑑xJ_{d_{2}}:=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}(d_{2}|\nabla v|^{2}+v^{2})dx-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\Omega}v^{p+1}_{+}dx

with v+=max⁡{v,0}v^{+}=\max\{v,0\}. Suppose that p∈(1,∞)p\in(1,\infty) if N=1,2N=1,2 and p∈(1,N+2N−2)p\in(1,\frac{N+2}{N-2}) if N≥3N\geq 3, Lin, Ni and Takagi [20] applied variational techniques and min–max arguments to prove that if d2d_{2} is small, (1.5) has only nonconstant positive least–energy solution, which is a critical point of Jd2J_{d_{2}} in H1​(Ω)H^{1}(\Omega). Furthermore, Ni and Takagi [28, 29] showed that the least–energy solutions must concentrate at a boundary spike if d2d_{2} is sufficiently small and the spike moves to the place of ∂Ω\partial\Omega with the largest mean curvature as d2d_{2} goes to zero. Motivated by their works, Grossi, Pistoia and Wei [9] obtained solutions of (1.5) with a single interior spike that stays in the most centered region of the domain (in the sense of a critical point of the distance function) for small d2d_{2}. By the Lyapunov-Schmidt method, Gui and Wei [10] construct multi-peak solutions with mm interior spikes and nn boundary spikes, for any nonnegative integers mm, nn, as long as d2d_{2} is sufficiently small. The methods and techniques used in these brilliant works began with good guesses on the structures of the spike(s). Moreover, the stability analysis has also been carried out through the infinite dimension Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction and the method of NLEP (nonlocal eigenvalue problem) recently developed by J. Wei, et al. See [32] and the surveys in [26, 27] for recent development in this direction.

It is worthwhile to point out that a large chemotactic coefficient χ\chi can also destabilize the constant solution of (1.4) like a small diffusion rate. Therefore, nontrivial steady states may emerge through large chemotactic coefficient χ\chi. For example, by taking χ\chi as the bifurcation parameter, Wang, et al. [4, 36, 37] applied global bifurcation methods to investigate nontrivial steady states of (1.4) over one–dimensional finite interval. Furthermore, these solutions are shown to admit boundary spikes or interior transition layers as χ\chi approaches infinity.

The logarithmic sensitivity function ϕ⁡(v)=ln⁡v\phi(v)=\ln v was chosen largely due to the Weber–Fechner’s law describing cellular behaviors: the subjective sensation is proportional to the logarithm of the stimulus intensity [12]. For the logarithmic model (1.4) with ϕ⁡(v)=ln⁡v\phi(v)=\ln v, we observe that the dynamics of cellular movements are dominated by the taxis flux χv∇v\frac{\chi}{v}\nabla v which may be unbounded for v≈0v\approx 0. We want to note that this singularity is an important mechanism in the formation of traveling wave solutions as showed in [16] or discussed in the survey paper [38]. See [21, 34] for more works on the logarithmic model. However, from the viewpoint of mathematical modeling, it is not reasonable to assume that low chemical concentration elicits significant chemotactic responses from the cell’s motility, hence we modify this problem by taking ϕ⁡(v)=ln⁡(v+c)\phi(v)=\ln(v+c) for a positive constant cc which saturates ϕ′​(v)\phi^{\prime}(v) at v=0v=0. Then the steady state of (1.4) becomes

{∇⋅(d1∇u−χu∇ln(v+c))=0,x∈Ω,d2​Δ​v−α​v+β​u=0,x∈Ω,∂u∂n=∂v∂n=0,x∈∂Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\nabla\cdot(d_{1}\nabla u-\chi u\nabla\ln(v+c))=0,&x\in\Omega,\\ d_{2}\Delta v-\alpha v+\beta u=0,&x\in\Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\textbf{n}}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\textbf{n}}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\end{array}\right. (1.6)

where d1d_{1}, d2d_{2}, χ\chi, cc, α\alpha and β\beta are positive constants. First of all, we claim that the total cell population in the time–dependent counterpart of (1.6) is conserved. Indeed, integrating the first equation over Ω\Omega, we have from the Neumann boundary conditions that

dd​t∫Ωu(x,t)dx=∫Ωut(x,t)dx=∫Ω∇⋅(d1∇u−χu∇ln(v+c))dx=0,\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)dx=\int_{\Omega}u_{t}(x,t)dx=\int_{\Omega}\nabla\cdot\Big(d_{1}\nabla u-\chi u\nabla\ln(v+c)\Big)dx=0,

and this implies that for all t>0t>0,

∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑x=∫Ωu⁡(x,0)​𝑑x=M.\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)dx=\int_{\Omega}u(x,0)dx=M. (1.7)

Throughout this paper, we assume the cell population in (1.7) is a fixed positive constant denoted by ∫Ωu⁡(x)​𝑑x=M\int_{\Omega}u(x)dx=M. Moreover, since small chemical diffusion rate supports nontrivial positive solutions to (1.6) as we shall show, we denote for the simplicity of notations that

ϵ2=d2α, and ​p=χd1,\epsilon^{2}=\frac{d_{2}}{\alpha},\text{~and~}p=\frac{\chi}{d_{1}},

then it is easy to see that (1.6) leads us to (1.1).

According to our results in Theorem 1.1, vϵ​(x)v_{\epsilon}(x) concentrates at the boundary point PϵP_{\epsilon} if the chemical diffusion rate ϵ\epsilon is sufficiently small. Compared to the spiky solutions in [20, 26, 27] and [32], vϵ​(x)v_{\epsilon}(x) has a boundary spike which is supported on a platform with height tϵ∗t^{*}_{\epsilon} in (1.2). The results in [20, 26, 27] and [32] are based on the application of the classical variational methods due to Ambrosetti and Rabinowitz [1] on the following equation,

d2Δv−v+f(v)=0,x∈Ω;∇v⋅n=0,x∈∂Ω,d_{2}\Delta v-v+f(v)=0,x\in\Omega;\nabla v\cdot\textbf{n}=0,~x\in\partial\Omega,

equipped with the energy functional

Jd2:=12​∫Ω(d2​|∇v|2+v2)​𝑑x−∫ΩF⁡(v)​𝑑x,F⁡(t)=∫0tf⁡(s)​𝑑s.J_{d_{2}}:=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}(d_{2}|\nabla v|^{2}+v^{2})dx-\int_{\Omega}F(v)dx,~F(t)=\int_{0}^{t}f(s)ds.

It is assumed, among other conditions, that f⁡(t)≡0f(t)\equiv 0 for t≤0t\leq 0 and f⁡(t)=o⁡(t)f(t)=o(t) as t→0+t\rightarrow 0^{+}. As we shall see later, system (1.1) can be reduced to the single equation (2.3), however, f⁡(v)f(v) there apparently does not satisfy these conditions, therefore it inhibits the direct application of the results in [20, 26, 27]. On the other hand, one needs some nontrivial modifications of the variational methods in [1] in order to apply them for (2.3). Furthermore, the nonlocal structure in (2.3) can not be scaled out as in [20] and this makes the application of previous results on (2.3) difficult. Therefore the adaption of the ideas in [20], etc. to (1.1) requires several technical tricks. Compared to the results obtained in [28, 29] and [32], where the sensitivity function is ϕ⁡(v)=ln⁡v\phi(v)=\ln v, our boundary spike is supported on a platform with height t∗>0t^{*}>0. If c=0c=0, we see from (1.2) that our results coincide with those obtained in [28, 29], except that the assumption on the initial cell population becomes M≤0M\leq 0, which apparently can not be true. However, we can consider an approximation problem with c≈0c\approx 0, then we can choose the parameters properly, for example α\alpha being large, such that both the assumption on the initial cell population MM and the smallness of ϵ\epsilon can be achieved.

We want to point out that the assumptions on MM and pp are made out of technical reasons. As we have discussed earlier, either small initial total cell mass or small chemo–attraction coefficient χ=p​d1\chi=pd_{1} tends to prevent solutions of (1.4) from blowing up in finite or infinite time, therefore it makes our analysis of pattern formations in the steady state realistic. It is also worthwhile to mention that the global existence of a parabolic–elliptic type system (1.4) with ϕ⁡(v)=ln⁡(v+c)\phi(v)=\ln(v+c) was studied in [3], and the fully parabolic system has been investigated in [35] for d1=d2=αd_{1}=d_{2}=\alpha provided that χ/d1=p<2/N\chi/d_{1}=p<\sqrt{2/N}, N≥2N\geq 2. However, the full understanding about its global existence or finite time blow–ups is away from complete and there are many problems widely left open. See the surveys [12, 14, 15]. Though our assumption on p=χ/d1p=\chi/d_{1} in Theorem 1.1 does not guarantee the global existence of the time–dependent systems, we surmise that the smallness assumption of the cell population might contribute in this matter.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we convert system (1.1) into a single equation with a nonlocal structure. Then we establish the existence of nontrivial positive solutions of the corresponding local problem. Section 3 is denoted to study the asymptotic behaviors of the positive solutions obtained in Section 2 as ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0. The proof of Theorem 1.1 is included at the end of this section. Finally, we present numerical simulations in Section 4 to illustrate and verify our numerical findings. Throughout the rest of this paper, we assume that CC and CiC_{i}, i=1,2,…i=1,2,... are generic positive constants that may vary from line to line.

2 Existence of nonconstant positive solutions

First of all, we observe that system (1.1) can be reduced to a single equation with an integral constraint. Indeed, we see that uu-equation in (1.1) is equivalent to

∇⋅(u∇(lnu−pln(v+c)))=0.\nabla\cdot\left(u\nabla\Big(\ln u-p\ln(v+c)\Big)\right)=0.

Testing it by ln⁡u−p​ln⁡(v+c)\ln u-p\ln(v+c) over Ω\Omega by parts, we have that

∫Ωu​|∇(ln⁡u−p​ln⁡(v+c))|2​𝑑x=0,\int_{\Omega}u\Big|\nabla\Big(\ln u-p\ln(v+c)\Big)\Big|^{2}dx=0,

therefore, there exists a positive constant CC such that

u=C​(v+c)pu=C(v+c)^{p} (2.1)

Integrating (2.1) over Ω\Omega leads us to

u=M​(v+c)p∫Ω(v+c)p​𝑑x,u=\frac{M(v+c)^{p}}{\int_{\Omega}(v+c)^{p}dx}, (2.2)

Proof.

Since fδ​(t)f_{\delta}(t) satisfies (2.12) and pp is subcritical, similar as the proof of Theorem 2 in [20], we can show that the least–energy value 𝒞ϵ,δ\mathcal{C}_{\epsilon,\delta} is achieved at wϵ​(x)w_{\epsilon}(x), which is a H1H^{1} solution to (2.8). 3 Single boundary spike on a platform

In this section, we construct a positive solution vϵ​(x)v_{\epsilon}(x) of (1.1) that has single boundary spike supported on a platform for ϵ\epsilon small. To this end, we first introduce the equation in the entire space, which we shall use to approximate least–energy solution wϵ,δ​(x)w_{\epsilon,\delta}(x) of (2.8).

Lemma 3.1.

For each δ∈(δ0,∞)\delta\in(\delta_{0},\infty), there exists a unique solution 𝐰δ\mathbf{w}_{\delta} to the following problem

{Δ​𝐰−cδ​𝐰+fδ​(𝐰)=0,x∈ℝN,𝐰(0)=maxx∈ℝN𝐰(x)>0,𝐰(x)>0,x∈ℝN,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\Delta\mathbf{w}-c_{\delta}\mathbf{w}+f_{\delta}(\mathbf{w})=0,&x\in{R}^{N},\\ \mathbf{w}(0)=\max_{x\in{R}^{N}}\mathbf{w}(x)>0,~\mathbf{w}(x)>0,&x\in{R}^{N},\end{array}\right. (3.1)

where cδc_{\delta} and fδf_{\delta} are the same as in (2.8). Moreover, 𝐰δ\mathbf{w}_{\delta} satisfies the followings:

(i) The solution 𝐰δ\mathbf{w}_{\delta} is radially symmetric such that, 𝐰δ​(x)=𝐰δ​(|x|)\mathbf{w}_{\delta}(x)=\mathbf{w}_{\delta}(|x|);

(ii) 𝐰δ′<0\mathbf{w}^{\prime}_{\delta}<0 for r>0r>0, with r=|x|r=|x|;

(iii) 𝐰δ​(r)≤C​e−μ​r\mathbf{w}_{\delta}(r)\leq Ce^{-\mu r}, r>1r>1, where CC and μ\mu are positive constants independent of δ\delta.

Furthermore, the system is associated with an energy functional Iδ​(𝐰)I_{\delta}(\mathbf{w}),

Iδ​(𝐰)=12​∫ℝN|∇𝐰|2+cδ​𝐰2​𝑑z−∫ℝNFδ​(𝐰)​𝑑z,I_{\delta}(\mathbf{w})=\frac{1}{2}\int_{{R}^{N}}|\nabla\mathbf{w}|^{2}+c_{\delta}\mathbf{w}^{2}dz-\int_{{R}^{N}}F_{\delta}(\mathbf{w})dz, (3.2)

which is positive and uniformly bounded in δ\delta.

Proof.

First of all, we see that for all δ∈(δ0,∞)\delta\in(\delta_{0},\infty)

(fδ​(t)t)′≥0, for all ​t≥0,\left(\frac{f_{\delta}(t)}{t}\right)^{\prime}\geq 0,\text{ for all }t\geq 0,

then by the celebrated Gidas–Ni–Nirenberg [8] symmetry theorem and the uniqueness result from Kwong and Zhang [19], there exists a unique solution 𝐰δ​(x)\mathbf{w}_{\delta}(x) to (3.1) which is radially symmetric. Choosing ϵ=1\epsilon=1 in the test function e⁡(x)e(x) defined in (2.11), we can show that Iδ​(𝐰δ)I_{\delta}(\mathbf{w}_{\delta}) is uniformly bounded in δ\delta by the similar proof as for (2.18), moreover there exists a positive constant CC independent of δ\delta such that

∥𝐰δ∥H1​(ℝN)<C,\lVert\mathbf{w}_{\delta}\rVert_{H^{1}({R}^{N})}<C,

Then we can apply the radial lemma of Strauss [33] to obtain that

|𝐰δ|≤C​r1−N2​∥𝐰δ∥H1​(ℝN),r≥1,\lvert\mathbf{w}_{\delta}\rvert\leq Cr^{\frac{1-N}{2}}\lVert\mathbf{w}_{\delta}\rVert_{H^{1}({R}^{N})},r\geq 1,

where CC is a positive constant which is independent of δ\delta. After applying Proposition 4.1 in [8] to (3.1), we have that

|𝐰δ|≤C​r1−N2​e−μ​r,\lvert\mathbf{w}_{\delta}\rvert\leq Cr^{\frac{1-N}{2}}e^{-\mu r},

and this concludes the proof of the lemma. □\mathchar 1027\relax

This unique solution 𝐰δ\mathbf{w}_{\delta} is called the ground state of (3.1). To study the least–energy solution wϵ,δ​(x)w_{\epsilon,\delta}(x) of (2.8), we note that fδ∈C1​(ℝ+,ℝ+)f_{\delta}\in C^{1}({R}^{+};{R}^{+}) and it satisfies fδ​(0)=0f_{\delta}(0)=0, fδ​(t)=o​(t)f_{\delta}(t)=o(t) as t→0+t\rightarrow 0^{+} and fδ​(t)=O⁡(tp)f_{\delta}(t)=O(t^{p}) as t→+∞t\rightarrow+\infty, where p∈(1,∞)p\in(1,\infty) if N=1,2N=1,2 and p∈(1,N+2(N−2))p\in(1,\frac{N+2}{(N-2)}) if N≥3N\geq 3. By the same arguments in the proof of Theorem 2.3 in [28] and Theorem 1.2 in [29], we can show the following results on the limiting profiles and single boundary spike of wϵ,δ​(x)w_{\epsilon,\delta}(x).

Proposition 3.

Let wϵ,δ​(x)w_{\epsilon,\delta}(x) be a least–energy solution to (2.8), i.e., a critical point of Jϵ,δJ_{\epsilon,\delta} in H1​(Ω)H^{1}(\Omega) such that Jϵ,δ​(wϵ,δ)=𝒞ϵ,δJ_{\epsilon,\delta}(w_{\epsilon,\delta})=\mathcal{C}_{\epsilon,\delta}, where 𝒞ϵ,δ\mathcal{C}_{\epsilon,\delta} is the least–energy value. H⁡(Pϵ)→maxΩ¯⁡H⁡(P), as ​ϵ→0.H(P_{\epsilon})\rightarrow\max_{\bar{\Omega}}H(P),\text{ as }\epsilon\rightarrow 0.

of Theorem 1.1. Let wϵ,δ​(x)w_{\epsilon,\delta}(x) be a least–energy solution obtained in Proposition 3. Following [32], we denote the set of least–energy solutions to (2.8) as

t1​(δ1)⋅|Ω|=m2,t_{1}(\delta_{1})\cdot\lvert\Omega\rvert=\frac{m}{2},

then it follows from (2.7) and (3.5) that

ρ⁡(δ1)=∫Ωvϵ,δ1​(x)​𝑑x=δ11p−1​∫Ωwϵ,δ1​(x)+t1​(δ1)​𝑑x=δ11p−1​ϵN​(12​∫ℝN𝐰δ1​𝑑z+o⁡(1))+m2.\begin{split}\rho(\delta_{1})&\left.=\int_{\Omega}v_{\epsilon,\delta_{1}}(x)dx=\delta_{1}^{\frac{1}{p-1}}\int_{\Omega}w_{\epsilon,\delta_{1}}(x)+t_{1}(\delta_{1})dx\right.\\ &\left.={\delta_{1}}^{\frac{1}{p-1}}\epsilon^{N}\left(\frac{1}{2}\int_{{R}^{N}}\mathbf{w}_{\delta_{1}}dz+o(1)\right)+\frac{m}{2}.\right.\end{split} (3.7)

ρ⁡(δϵ)=∫Ωvϵ,δϵ​(x)​𝑑x=m, thus ​δϵ=∫Ω(vϵ,δϵ​(x)+c)p​𝑑x.\rho(\delta_{\epsilon})=\int_{\Omega}v_{\epsilon,\delta_{\epsilon}}(x)dx=m,\text{ thus }\delta_{\epsilon}=\int_{\Omega}(v_{\epsilon,\delta_{\epsilon}}(x)+c)^{p}dx.

4 Numerical simulations of spiky solutions

In this section, we present numerical results on the the formation and evolution of boundary spike of (1.4) over Ω=(0,1)×(0,1)\Omega=(0,1)\times(0,1) to illustrate our theoretical results. Putting α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1, and ϕ⁡(v)=ln⁡(v+c)\phi(v)=\ln(v+c), we perform extensive numerical simulations on (1.4) by choosing different sets of values for ϵ\epsilon, cc and the initial data. We shall see that multi–spike solutions also arise through the system. It is worthwhile to mention that rigorous analysis is needed to fully understand the dynamics such as the large time behaviors and stability of these structures, which is beyond the scope of this paper.

For c=0.1c=0.1, numerical simulations of system (1.4) on the unit square are plotted in Figure 1. The graphes in the first line represent the spatial–temporal behaviors of the cellular population density u⁡(x,y,t)u(x,y,t) and the graphes in the second line illustrate the behaviors of the chemical concentration v⁡(x,y,t)v(x,y,t). Our simulations show that uu quickly develops an interior spike which gradually moves to the corner. Eventually a stable spike is formed at the boundary point corner (0,0)(0,0), where the boundary is most curved.

In Figure 2, we choose c=5c=5 and take the same initial data and system parameters as in Figure 1. For this set of values, solutions quickly evolves into a boundary spike at t=100t=100 compared to that in Figure 1. It eventually develops into a stable boundary spike concerned at (0,0)(0,0). We find through our numerical results that the stable boundary spike stays on a platform with height 0.02, compared with those obtained in Figure 1. According to our steady state analysis, we surmise that this platform is contributed by the large magnitude of cc. We need to point out that our numerical results are ambiguous since the height of the platform for Figure 2 is t∗=β​Mα​|Ω|=3t^{*}=\frac{\beta M}{\alpha|\Omega|}=3, which is greatly larger than 0.02. However, the numerical simulations support our analysis qualitatively and rigorous stability analysis is needed to fully understand the dynamics of the spiky solutions. We also perform numerical simulations in Figure 3 which show that the constant solution is a global attractor of (1.4) if cc is sufficiently large, independent of the initial data. This corresponds to the fact that the saturating coefficient cc in (1.1) reduces the chemo–attraction magnitude and stabilizes the positive constant steady state.

We proceed to simulate the formations of stable interior spike and multi–spikes in Figure 4. Our goal is to illustrate the effect of initial data on the localization of the spikes, i.e., the spot where a spike is formed. To this end, we choose different initial data in Figure 4. The initial data on the left are taken to be u0​(x,y)=3−cos⁡(π​x)​cos⁡(π​y)−cos⁡(π⁡(x−1))​cos⁡(π⁡(y−1))u_{0}(x,y)=3-\cos(\pi x)\cos(\pi y)-\cos(\pi(x-1))\cos(\pi(y-1)), v0​(x,y)=3+cos⁡(π⁡(x−1/2))​cos⁡(π⁡(y−1/2))v_{0}(x,y)=3+\cos(\pi(x-1/2))\cos(\pi(y-1/2)), where the initial chemical concentration v0v_{0} attains its maximum at point (1/2,1/2)(1/2,1/2). We see that a stable interior spike is formed at this point. The initial data on the right are u0​(x,y)=3−cos⁡(π​x)​cos⁡(π​y)−cos⁡(π⁡(x−1))​cos⁡(π⁡(y−1))u_{0}(x,y)=3-\cos(\pi x)\cos(\pi y)-\cos(\pi(x-1))\cos(\pi(y-1)), v0​(x,y)=3+cos⁡(π​x)​cos⁡(π​y)+cos⁡(π⁡(x−1))​cos⁡(π⁡(y−1))v_{0}(x,y)=3+\cos(\pi x)\cos(\pi y)+\cos(\pi(x-1))\cos(\pi(y-1)) and v0v_{0} achieves its maximum at two boundary points (0,0)(0,0) and (1,1)(1,1). Then a stable double boundary spike is developed at both maximum points. Our numerical simulations indicate that the spike of (1.4) with saturated logarithmic sensitivity can localize at the spot where the initial chemical concentration reaches its largest value, independent of the initial cellular population distribution. This complies with the well–accepted theoretical results that chemotaxis dominates the dynamics of the cellular movements over the domain when χ\chi is not too small or cc is not too large. However, a rigorous analysis for this purpose requires totally non–trivial mathematical techniques.

Finally, we present Figure 5 to illustrate the emergence of multi–spikes in model (1.4) with parameters taken to be d1=1d_{1}=1, d2=0.001d_{2}=0.001, χ=3\chi=3 and α=β=c=1\alpha=\beta=c=1. The initial data are u0​(x,y)=3+0.1​cos⁡(π​x)​cos⁡(π​y)u_{0}(x,y)=3+0.1\cos(\pi x)\cos(\pi y) and v0​(x,y)=3+cos⁡(2​π​x)​cos⁡(2​π​y)v_{0}(x,y)=3+\cos(2\pi x)\cos(2\pi y). We observe that both uu and vv develop multi–spikes (t=100t=100) at the four corners and the center very quickly. The structures of these multi–spikes keep well–preserved for quite a long time period (through t=100t=100 to t=300t=300), then four spikes at the corner disappear and both uu and vv develop into a stable interior spike at the center eventually. Our numerical simulations illustrate that the multi–spikes can arise from system (1.4) and they are always unstable or meta–stable. The rigorous stability analysis is beyond the scope of this paper. Figure 5 also suggests that the formation of stable patterns, i.e., solutions with spikes or stripes, etc., depends on the initial data and in particular the initial distribution of chemical concentration.

I want to thank the anonymous referee for carefully reading this paper and giving insightful comments and constructive suggestions which improved its exposition. This work was partially supported by the Summer Research Fund from the Math Department of Tulane University. This research also receives support from the Project–sponsored by SRF for ROCS, SEM.
